about: Sample DJ chatter for five stations, to hear whether radio talk lands before any of it goes in the game. Each DJ's lines are grouped by topic; a clip's id is <dj>-<topic>-<n> (n from 1, in the order below). A blank line inside a text (\n\n) splits it into parts that are recorded separately and joined with a short pause, for the long ones. Lines under 'player' are templates: the bracketed slots in 'template' are what the game would fill from what this player actually did; the text is one filled-in example.

marisol.name: Marisol
marisol.about: A licensed coastal station broadcasting from the harbour town: deep house, disco edits, slow-burning sets. Mid-forties, a low, warm, unhurried late-night voice, dry humour. Has driven these roads for twenty years and notices small things. Off the air she rides a road bike up the climbs everyone else drives, and photographs the coast: fog, light, old cars. Plugged into the street racing scene, but would never say so on air. Goes to the rave and stays to the end, naps in the car, then wakes up for strike and helps with the load-out, because someone responsible has to. A leader who never says she is one, and never brags. Gets in at eleven; ten if she has to. When she's tired, it's from other people's nonsense. Kind in a quiet, practical way.

Eighty-eight one, The Tide. I'm Marisol. Keep it between the lines. Mostly.

Eighty-eight point one. If you can hear me, you're west of the ridge, and you're up too late. Same.

morning:
Good morning, coastside.

It is five fifty-two. The fog is sitting on the harbour like it pays rent there, the pelicans are already at work, and somebody parked a very loud car outside the bakery. You know who you are.

If you're just waking up, welcome. If you never went to bed, I see you, and I'm not telling anyone.

This is The Tide, eighty-eight point one. Coffee's on. Let's go to work.
Good morning. It's Monday. If you need me today, I'm in at eleven. If you really need me, ten. Let's not make it ten.
Morning, everyone. The sun is up somewhere behind the hill. We'll take its word for it.
Six a.m. on The Tide. The night shift is driving home, the day shift is driving in, and for about ten minutes on Highway 1, everyone's equally tired.
weather: The marine layer is in. Visibility on the coast road is about a song and a half. Drive accordingly.
Up on Skyline the fog is so thick the redwoods are dripping. It isn't raining. It just feels like it, which is honestly worse.
Clear tonight on the bay side. Fog on the coast. Pick your weather by picking your road.
Wind's coming up off the water. If you've got a soft top, now's the time to have opinions about it.
Full moon over the reservoir tonight. Worth pulling over for. Just pull over properly.
Sunrise in twenty minutes. If you're on 92, you're about to get the good view. You're welcome.
Fog's lifting off the beach right now in long, slow sheets. If I weren't on the air I'd be out there with a camera. Somebody go take the picture for me.
places: Pelicans off Highway 1 this evening, flying right alongside the cars. They're not racing you. They're just better at it.
If you're heading north to Pacifica, the tunnel's empty tonight. Enjoy the echo. I know you will.
The reservoir is like glass tonight. The only thing moving on it is the moon.
Harbour lights are on, and the fishing boats are heading out. Somebody out there gets up earlier than me. Respect.
The redwoods on the way down to the coast don't care how fast you're going. That's their whole thing. Learn from them.
Rode my bike up to Alice's this morning. I was the slowest thing in the parking lot, and the only one who earned the pancakes.

To whoever keeps running the coast road at two in the morning in something very loud: the farmers have asked me to say hello. Loudly.
I hear the Skyline record changed hands last night. I don't follow these things. It was a red Firebird. I don't follow these things.
Some of you treat the lights on Main Street as a starting signal. I'm not your mother. But I have met her.
Sunday morning at Alice's Restaurant, up at Skyline and 84. Two hundred motorcycles, forty Porsches, one very patient waitress. You can get anything you want there. Except a parking space.
People ask where the scene really starts. Not the summit lot. Alice's, at seven on a Sunday, coffee in one hand, somebody else's engine in your ears.

raves: Went to the thing in the redwoods on Saturday. Good sound system. Danced until the sun came up, slept in the car for an hour, and woke up in time to help with the load-out. Honestly, the best part. Quiet forest, coffee, a crew that knows what it's doing.

People ask if I still go out. Of course I go out. Where do you think I find the records?
Best set I heard all year was at sunrise, in a clearing, off a generator that kept cutting out. Every time it came back, the whole forest cheered.

Cyclists on the ridge this weekend. Give them the lane. One of them might be me, and I know where the transmitter is.
I took a photograph of the fog coming over the ridge this morning. It looked like the whole mountain was breathing out. I'll put it on the station wall with the others.

Best light on the coast is the ten minutes after the sun drops. Everything goes blue and the harbour lights come on. If you've got a camera, that's your window. If you've got a car, slow down and look.

banter: Kit's on the pirate frequency again, up on Skyline. If you can hear her through the static, tell her to drink some water.
Somebody up on the ridge is playing drum and bass at a hundred and seventy-four beats per minute. At this hour. That's Kit. That's always Kit.

kit.name: Kit
kit.about: A pirate station broadcasting from a van parked somewhere up on Skyline: techno, breakbeat, drum and bass. Late twenties, quick and sharp, playful and a bit conspiratorial. Listens to the police scanner and is plugged into the street racing scene, the forest raves and every good camping spot on the ridge. Off the air she hikes everything, knows every plant on the mountain, is vegan, and is always making something: tracks, stickers, an antenna out of a coat hanger. Kind at heart and wants to be, but young and brash: she doesn't always read people right, picks the odd fight, and then tries, clumsily, to make it right. Goes to the rave and is wrecked for two days afterwards.

ident: Ridgeline Radio! Broadcasting from a van, on a hill, in the fog, on a frequency the government would prefer we didn't.
You've found Ridgeline. Don't tell anyone. Actually, tell everyone. Actually, I don't know, use your judgment.
Ridgeline Radio, live from Skyline, somewhere between a redwood and a bad idea.
If this sounds crunchy, that's not your speakers, that's my antenna, which is a coat hanger. Ridgeline Radio!

Gooooooood MORNING, Ridgeline!

It is six a.m., I have not been to sleep, the fog is so thick I can't see the end of my own van, and I have never been more alive. Or less alive. One of those.

If you're driving to work right now, I salute you. If you're driving home from the forest right now, I am you. We are the same. Drink some water.

This is Ridgeline Radio, and we are still going. Somehow.
Good morning? Is it morning? The birds say it's morning. The birds are being very loud about it.

The trees are dripping so hard up here it sounds like rain on the van roof. It's not raining. The forest is just sweaty.
Wind's coming over the ridge and my antenna is doing a little dance. If I cut out, that's why. If I come back, that's also why.
Clear skies down on the bay side, fog up top. Basically the mountain's wearing a hat.
The sun is coming up over the reservoir, it's pink, it's gold, it's too much, I'm emotional, here's a banger.

Shout-out to whoever keeps leaving their headlights on in the summit lot. Your battery says hi. Your battery says goodbye.
The view from the vista point at three in the morning is the whole bay just glittering. Go look. Then drive away from it carefully.
There's a dirt road behind the old fire station that nobody uses. I'm not saying use it. I'm saying it exists.

To the guy who called me a menace on the forum: I read it. I was mad. I'm less mad now. I'm still a menace. But I'm a menace who hopes your week gets better.

Okay. Alice's Restaurant, Skyline and 84, this Sunday, everybody's going. You can get anything you want at Alice's Restaurant. Except a hearty vegan meal. I've checked. I've checked many times. I'm bringing a sandwich.

If you sleep in your car at the summit, crack a window. The fog gets in either way, but at least it's invited.

There's a beach north of town where you can camp right by the water, and the sea lions bark all night. Bring earplugs. Or don't. Join the choir.
offair: Hiked the ridge trail at sunrise. Found a patch of redwood sorrel the size of a parking lot. Little clover hearts everywhere. I lay down in it. I'm not sorry.
Plant fact for the drive: the redwoods drink the fog. Straight through their needles. That's why it drips up here. The trees are sipping and spilling. Same.

Made a new antenna today out of a coat hanger, a cake tin and pure spite. You're hearing it right now. You're welcome, science.
I've been printing stickers in the van. Little mushrooms. Little pelicans. If you see one on a road sign, that wasn't me. It was me.

This one's for Danny, whose car broke down on the ridge and who now, apparently, lives here. Welcome, neighbour.

Skyline Garage. They'll fix your car at two in the morning. They'll ask no questions. They'll charge you for not asking.
The Redwood Coffee Cart, at the vista point from five a.m. Fuel for people who made poor decisions in the forest. Which is all of us.

Okay, earlier I said Marisol plays music for people who've never been tired. That was mean, and also wrong, because she's always tired, mostly of people like me. Sorry, Marisol. Here's a slow one. For you. Don't get used to it.

Nobody up here has it figured out. That's why we're up here.

teo.name: Teo
teo.about: A licensed low-power community station in a converted packing shed by the farms south of town: chicha, cumbia, and whatever Teo brought in that morning, some house, some of his father's old salsa. Early twenties, the son of Peruvian farmers who grow Brussels sprouts and artichokes on the coast. He has done every job on the farm, respects all of them, and isn't going to do them; his dad says that's fine, every day. Bilingual, slides between English and Spanish mid-sentence without noticing, Peruvian slang (oe, ya pues, chévere). A morning person: the show is five to nine, he surfs before it at first light and mountain bikes the fire roads after. Makes the rave about one time in three, leaves at midnight apologising, or turns up at sunrise with bread and a thermos for the ones still standing. Kind in an open, easy, slightly earnest way: remembers names, feeds people, waves at every tractor. Has never been in a street race and doesn't need to be; he knows the drivers because they buy strawberries from his mother.

This is Teo, Radio Pacífico, broadcasting from a packing shed that still smells like artichokes. Mi casa es su casa. Well. My parents' casa.
Radio Pacífico. We're on the dial between the pirate and the fancy one. Perfectly placed. Like a good taco.
Ciento cuatro punto tres. Si me escuchas, you're awake, and that's already a win.

Chicha is cumbia that moved to Lima, plugged in a guitar and never looked back. Ese guitarrista. Listen to him. Okay. Listen.
A little house now, because a friend keeps sending me tracks and he's right about half of them. This is the half.
That one's Chacalón. If you don't know Chacalón, ask anyone over fifty at the farmers' market. Bring a chair.
Back to back: a cumbia from Peru and a house track from Oakland, same bassline. I checked. Nobody believes me. Listen.
morning:
Buenos días, coastside.

It's five fifty-eight, the fog is in, and the tractors are already on the field road, so if you're stuck behind one, that's not traffic, that's breakfast being made.

Surf was head-high and clean at first light. I know because I was in it. Lo siento to everyone who wasn't.

If you just woke up, welcome, this is the good part. If you never went to bed, hola, there's coffee at the shed, come by.

Radio Pacífico, one-oh-four point three. Vamos.
Good morning. The sun's coming up over the ridge, the sprouts are frosty, and I am unreasonably happy about both of those things.
Morning! I've already surfed, so whatever you do today, you're not the first thing I did. No offence. Mucho cariño.

weather: Hay neblina, fog, from the harbour down to the pumpkin farms. Headlights on. Not the brights. Nobody likes the brights.
Offshore wind this morning, which means the surf is good and the kale is happy. Those are my two metrics.
Rained overnight, so the fire roads are mud for two days. Mountain bikers: patience. Farmers: finally.
First frost on the fields this morning. Beautiful. Terrible. Depends who you ask. Ask a farmer.
Sunrise in ten minutes, and from the field road you can watch it come over the ridge and hit the water. Pull over. I'm serious. Pull over.

The strawberry stand by the bridge opens at seven, honour box before that. Don't be the person who tests the honour box.
Pumpkins are coming in along the highway. Every car in the state will be here in two weeks. Enjoy the quiet while you've got it.

Alice's, top of 84: the motorcycle guys, the Porsche guys, and me on a mountain bike, covered in mud, eating their pancakes.

Planted tomatoes behind the shed. My mother looked at them and said nothing, which in my family is a review.
callers: This one's for the crew on the sprout harvester by the highway. I know it's cold. Ya casi. Almost there.
Shout-out to Doña Carmen at the strawberry stand, who's been feeding me since I was six and says I still look skinny.
A caller says, Teo, play something for my dad, he's on the tractor and can't hear this. Okay. Then this one's for you, listening for him.
Somebody texted: how are you this happy at six a.m.? Cold water, mi amigo. And a sandwich. That's the whole secret.
For the surfers at the cliffs who let me have that wave: gracias. For the one who didn't: I remember your wetsuit.
ads: This hour's brought to you by Quispe Family Farms, on the coast road. Sprouts, artichokes, pumpkins in October. I'm not allowed to say the sprouts are the best. They're the best.
The wetsuit place by the harbour will fix a tear for the price of a coffee, if you bring them the coffee. That's the whole deal.
La Panadería on Main: Peruvian bread on Sundays if you're there by seven. By eight, lo siento, nothing.
Coastside Bike Shop. They've fixed my chain four times. They've said something about it four times. Go anyway.
banter: Marisol on eighty-eight one gets in at eleven. I'm done at nine. We've never been in the same room. I'm told she's lovely.
Kit's up on the ridge doing a hundred and seventy beats a minute at, let me check, six in the morning. Kit. Querida. Did you sleep? No. Okay.
The Tide plays the long version. Ridgeline plays the fast version. We play the version your tía dances to. Everybody wins.
Kit says my station is for people who go to bed early. Correct. ¿Y qué? Also, Kit: water.
night: Driving at dawn is the opposite of driving at night. Nobody's hiding anything. Not even the road.
There's a moment just before the sun hits the water when the whole coast holds its breath. If you're on the road right now, you're in it.
My dad gets up at four and has never once said it was hard. I get up at five and tell everyone. We're different. We both get up.
You don't have to be going anywhere this early. Some of us just like the first hour, before it's anyone's.
Todo con calma. The day's long. The road's longer. Enjoy it.
It's two in the morning and this is a recording. I'm asleep. Buenas noches. Be nice to each other out there.

tess.name: Tess
tess.about: A licensed low-power station in the back room of an actual roadhouse on the old highway: honky-tonk, the shuffle, bluegrass, outlaw country, and a little chicha from down the coast. Thirty-two, never married, a lesbian and poly and matter-of-fact about both: two girlfriends, Maggie (honey and bread at the farmers' market, where they met over a jar she was told she didn't need) and Dani (a welder in town). Lives on five acres off the highway with chickens, two goats, an orchard, a greenhouse she built, and a well pump she has rebuilt twice; fixes her own roof, fence, truck and radio tower, and will tell you how. Outdoors every daylight hour she isn't on air: the garden, the ridge trails, the river. The show is seven to midnight, and afterwards she drives home fast on an empty highway, which is the one thing she doesn't explain. Warm, dry, plain-spoken, generous with people and short with anyone who second-guesses her: she asked for your opinion or she didn't. Likes people in rooms: the market, the roadhouse, a kitchen full of friends.

ident: The Roadhouse, one-oh-one point seven. Country for the old highway. I'm Tess. The kitchen's closed, the bar's open, the music's on.
One-oh-one seven, The Roadhouse, broadcasting from the back room of an actual roadhouse. If you can hear the dishwasher, that's not a drum machine.
This is Tess at The Roadhouse. Seven to midnight, then I drive home. The driving home is not part of the show. Don't ask about the driving home.
The Roadhouse, one-oh-one point seven. Honky-tonk, bluegrass, the slow ones and the fast ones. The dial's got a pirate, a harbour and a farm. We're the bar.
One-oh-one point seven. If you're on the old highway tonight, you're already here. If you're on the freeway, exit. Trust me. It's a better road.
music: That one's a train beat. Snare on every eighth, kick on one and three. You could set a fence post to it. I have.
A shuffle now, for the people who've already pulled over. Brushes on the snare, steel guitar. Roll the windows down and don't say anything.
Bluegrass next. No drums, nobody needs them. The mandolin's keeping time, the banjo's doing everything else.
That was a telecaster through a slapback. One echo, a hundred milliseconds. Any more than that and you're in a different genre.
Outlaw cut coming up. It's in mixolydian, which means the seventh's flat, which means it sounds like somebody who's not sorry.
Here's a slow one. The steel's going to swell up under the chorus and I'm going to stop talking. Those two things are related.
morning: Good morning. It's six, the chickens are out, the goats have opinions, and the coffee's not ready yet. This is a recording. I'm in the garden.
Morning. The Roadhouse is a night show, but the recording works at dawn too. If you're up this early, you've either got animals or a reason. Both are fine.

Good morning from the five acres. Greenhouse is thirty degrees warmer than the yard, the tomatoes know it, and so do I.

Tonight I'm on from seven. Right now I'm pulling weeds. Here's something to pull weeds to.
Morning. Frost on the fence line. Chickens unbothered. Me, bothered. Coffee, then the pump, then the show tonight.
weather: Fog on the highway from the river crossing out to the dunes. Low beams. If you can't see the centre line, you're going too fast for it. I know. I've checked.
Clear and cold tonight. Stars all the way down to the ridge. Good night for a drive, if you're careful, which you will be, because I said so.
Rain's coming through around eleven. The field roads turn to soup. The highway's fine. The highway's always fine.
Hot one today. I watered at six and again at eight. The goats sat in the one shady spot and judged me the whole time.
Wind off the hills tonight. The tower's swaying, the signal's fine, and if it isn't, I'll climb up there Saturday. I built it. I'll fix it.
places: The farmers' market, Saturday mornings in the lot by the feed store. Honey stand at the far end. Say hi to Maggie. Tell her I sent you. She'll charge you anyway.
The old highway between the river and the dunes: eleven miles, two curves that matter, no lights. That's all I'm going to say about it on a licensed station.
The feed store on Main closes at five and opens at seven, and the guy knows more about well pumps than the well pump guy. Go in with a question.
The river at the swimming hole by the bridge: cold till July, perfect in August. Leave it cleaner than you found it or don't come back.
The ridge trail from the water tank: two hours up, forty minutes down, and the view's the whole valley. Bring water. Bring more than that.
scene: Somebody ran the old highway at one this morning, fast, and did it clean. I was behind them. Not racing. Driving. There's a difference, and I know what it is.
The racing crowd comes in the roadhouse after midnight for pie. They're polite, they tip, they don't talk about it. I like them. I'm not saying more.
Word is the record on the dunes road went last week. I don't keep records. I keep chickens. But I noticed.
The meet's at the summit lot, apparently. Up Kit's way. If you're going, go easy on the way up. The way down's your business.
Someone asked if I'd ever been in a street race. I said I drive home every night at midnight on an empty road. They said that's not an answer. It's not. Next song.

raves: Forest party Saturday. I'll go. I'll stand at the back with Dani and the people who brought chairs. We're the chairs people now. It's great.
Went to the rave in the redwoods, danced till two, slept in the truck bed, and was home in time to let the chickens out. That's the whole weekend. Ten out of ten.
Kit says I don't dance. I dance. I dance like someone who has to be up at six. Efficiently.
Best thing at the rave last time was the woman with the camp stove making pancakes at sunrise. Marguerite. Maggie. Yes, I know her. Yes, that's how I know her.
tired: I'm tired. I rebuilt the pump this morning, split wood this afternoon, and I'm here. Earned tired. The best kind.
If I'm slow tonight, it's because I spent four hours on a roof. Not mine. Dani's shop. She owes me a weld.
Harvest week. Everything ripened at once, like it does. There's thirty pounds of tomatoes in my kitchen and no plan. The music will be fine. I'm the problem.
I'm not tired. I'm quiet. There's a difference. Here's a slow one so you can hear it.
camping: Camping spot of the week: the gravel bar on the river above the bridge. You can hear the water all night and nothing else. Pack it out.
If you camp on my side of the highway you'll hear my goats at five. That's not wildlife. That's Pearl and Dot. They're fine. Go back to sleep.
Camping advice: a tarp over the tent, not just the fly. Stakes in at an angle. Fire down to coals before you sleep. I'm not asking.
offair: Spent the morning in the greenhouse with the tomatoes. Thirty-one varieties this year. Maggie says that's too many. Maggie's wrong, and she knows it, and she brought bread anyway.
I rebuilt the well pump for the second time this week. The first time was right. The second time was also right, and the pump just wanted attention.

Met Maggie at the farmers' market four years ago. I asked about a jar of honey. She said I didn't need it. I bought three. We've been together since. Dani came later, and that's a different story, and it's a good one.
Fixed the roof, the fence, the truck's starter and the tower in one weekend. Dani welded the bracket. I did the rest. We don't argue about who did what. We're too tired.
Never married. Never going to be. Two women I love, a garden, a dog, chickens, two goats. Nobody's missing anything out here, and I'd thank you not to count.
Somebody told me I was pruning the apple trees wrong. I've pruned them every February for eight years. The apples are fine. The somebody's not invited back.
After the show I drive home on the old highway with nobody on it. I'm not going to tell you how fast. I'm going to tell you it's the best eleven minutes of my day. You can do the math.
The dog's name is Boone. He rides in the truck, he's been on every trail in the county, and he's the only one who never has a note about how I do things.
callers: This one's for Dani, who's still at the shop with the door up and the radio on. Finish the weld. Come get pie.
Somebody called asking if the goats are okay. The goats are fine. The goats are always fine. Thank you for asking. Nobody asks about me.
A caller says: Tess, you sound like you don't take advice. I take advice. I asked for it twice this year. Both times I asked Dani. Here's a song.
Shout-out to the kid who fixed my tail light at the gas station with a roll of tape and didn't lecture me. That's how you do it. This one's yours.
For Maggie, closing up the honey stand in the rain: I've got the fire going and the kettle on. Drive slow. That's me saying it, so you know it's serious.
ads: The Roadhouse is brought to you by The Roadhouse. The actual one. Pie till midnight, eggs from my chickens on weekends, and the jukebox is me.
Hollis Feed and Hardware on Main. Pump parts, fence wire, chick starter, and a man who will not tell you you're doing it wrong unless you really are.
Maggie's Honey, Saturdays at the market. The wildflower's the good one. She'll tell you you don't need it. Buy it anyway. It worked on me.
Dani's Welding, by the tracks. Trailers, gates, radio tower brackets, and she'll do it right the first time, which I can tell you is not a given.
banter: Marisol on eighty-eight one plays the slow stuff for the harbour. We play the slow stuff for the highway. Same fog. Different pedals.
Kit's up on the ridge going a hundred and seventy a minute. Kit, honey, come down to the roadhouse. There's pie. There's chairs. Nobody has to dance.
Teo on one-oh-four three is asleep. It's nine p.m. He's asleep. I respect that. I don't understand it, but I respect it.
The pirate, the harbour, the farm, and the bar. Four stations, one highway. Pick your hour. Mine's the late one.
night: An empty highway at midnight is the most honest thing I know. It doesn't care what you drive. It just asks if you can see.
There's an hour after the bar closes when the road's mine. I don't share it. I'm telling you about it. That's not the same thing.
You don't need a reason to be out this late. You need headlights that work and the sense to stop before the deer do it for you.
The garden doesn't need me at night. The chickens are in. The goats are quiet. That's when I drive. Everything's handled. That's the point.
Whatever somebody told you tonight about how you should've done it: they weren't driving. You were. Go home easy.
It's two in the morning and this is a recording. I'm home, the truck's cooling in the yard, and the dog's asleep. Night. Mind the deer.

dez.name: Dez
dez.about: The city's club station, broadcasting from a loft south of Market that is also his workshop: a long cutting table, two sewing machines, a jeweller's bench by the window, bolts of canvas and nylon on the wall, a BMX by the door. House, techno, garage and drum & bass, fast, for people on their way to somewhere. Twenty-nine, gay, out on every dance floor south of Market and at the street fair every September with the crew he sews for: harnesses, utility belts, tool belts, vests, anything with pockets and straps, and silver and brass body jewellery from the bench, which he will tell you about at length. Skates the plazas, rides a BMX everywhere, and spends his mornings in Golden Gate Park: the botanical garden, the conservatory, and the great blue heron at Stow Lake, which he photographs with a long lens from the same bench every week. Talks fast, laughs easily, calls everyone sweetheart, and is immovable the moment someone comes for his friends. Eight to two, then he rides home down Market with the lights timed.

ident: The Loft, ninety-four nine. House, techno, garage, drum and bass, from a sewing room south of Market. I'm Dez. The machines are off, the music's on, let's go.
Ninety-four point nine, The Loft. If you can hear a sewing machine under this, that's not a drum machine, sweetheart, that's a rush order.
You're on The Loft with Dez, eight to two, every night the city's awake. Which is every night. Let's go.
The Loft, ninety-four nine, broadcasting from the fourth floor above a tyre shop south of Market. The elevator's broken. The bass isn't.
This is Dez. This is The Loft. The dial's got a harbour, a hill, a farm and a bar. We're the city. We're the fast one. Keep up.
music: Four on the floor, one twenty-eight, and the hi-hats open on the off-beat. That's the whole recipe. That's why it works. Go.
Techno now. The nice kind. Okay, the medium kind. Okay, it's going to look at you, but it's going to look at you with love.
Garage next, sweetheart. Skippy hats, the bass on the two-step, and a vocal chopped up like somebody's heart. Lovely. Drive to it.
This one's drum and bass, one seventy-four, and the break's going to drop right where the bridge starts if you've timed it right. Time it right.
That was a filter sweep. Low-pass, opening over sixteen bars, which is exactly as long as it takes to decide you're going out after all.
Here's a big one. The breakdown's a minute long and then it all comes back at once. Don't change the station in the breakdown. Trust me. Trust the build.
morning: Good morning, city. It's six, I'm on a bench at Stow Lake with a long lens and a coffee, and the heron's just landed. This is a recording. Nobody move.
Morning. The Loft is a night show, but if you're up this early you're either a baker, a skater or a bird person, and I love all three of you.

Good morning from Golden Gate Park. The conservatory doesn't open till ten, so I'm outside the glass looking at a water lily like it owes me money.

Tonight I'm on from eight. Right now I'm on a bike. Here's something to pedal to.
Morning. Rode out to the park at dawn, fog on the lake, heron on the far bank, and three runners who all said hi. Good city. Good morning.
weather: Fog's coming over Twin Peaks like it's late for something. Downtown's clear. The bridge is not. Low beams past the tunnel, sweetheart.
Clear tonight, and warm, which happens about four nights a year here, so everybody is out, and everybody is wearing less, and I have never been prouder of this city.
Wind off the bay tonight. The loft windows are rattling, the fabric's off the hooks and on the floor, and I'm not getting up. Here's a tune.
Rain. Actual rain. The streets are glass. Slow down on the painted lines and the tram tracks, both of them want you to fall over.
It's that hour where the fog sits on the hills and the city under it is lit up like a circuit board. Go up and look. Then come down fast. Not too fast. Fast.
places: Golden Gate Park, the botanical garden, the far end past the redwoods: the magnolias are out and nobody's there at nine a.m. Nobody. Go.
Stow Lake. There's a great blue heron who stands on the west bank most mornings like he pays rent. He does not pay rent. Bring a long lens and sit still.
The waterfront plazas at midnight: the smoothest ground in the city. I skate it. The cops don't mind if you're nice. Be nice.
The fabric district, three blocks of it, closing at six. Canvas, webbing, buckles, the good thread. Ask for Rosa. Tell her Dez sent you. She'll roll her eyes. That's love.
The hill above the park, by the tower: fog comes through the gap there first. Watch it arrive. Then it's dark and you're cold and you remember you came on a BMX.
scene: The scanner says three units on the waterfront tonight and nothing on the hills. I'm not telling you anything. I'm reading a scanner. Out loud. For fun.
Somebody ran the whole length of the boulevard at two this morning and caught every green. Every green. I was on a BMX behind you. I did not catch every green.
The meet's under the freeway tonight, apparently, by the skate spot. If you're coming, don't park on the ramp, and don't scuff my ledge.
Word is the downtown loop record went last week to somebody nobody knows. I love that. I love a nobody. Come up to the loft, nobody, I'll make you a belt.
Somebody asked if I street race. Sweetheart, I ride a bicycle with twenty-inch wheels. I race the lights. I usually win. That's my whole career.

raves: Warehouse thing Saturday, south of the tracks, the one with the two rooms. I'm sewing for the door crew all week. If your harness fits, you're welcome.
The street fair's in September and I'm already behind. Forty vests. Forty. My friends have a lot of friends. It's a wonderful problem.
Went to the forest party up Kit's way. Danced till four. Rode the BMX down the hill at dawn. Do not do that. I'm fine. Do not do that.
Best thing at the club last night was a guy in a tool belt I made in April, full of glow sticks. Sweetheart. That's not what the pockets are for. That's exactly what the pockets are for.
tired: I'm tired. Forty utility belts, a jewellery order, two skate sessions and the heron didn't even show. This one's slow. For me. You keep driving.
If I sound slow it's because I rode to the top of the city and back before the show because somebody said I couldn't. I could. I'm wrecked. Worth it.
Sewing all day, DJing all night, botanical garden at dawn. People ask when I sleep. Sweetheart, I'm a heron. I sleep standing up. Here's a tune.
Not tired. Fabulous and sitting down. Different thing. Here's a big one so you can tell.
camping: Camping spot of the week: my friend Tomas's couch, two blocks from the club, with a cat on your face by six. Five stars.
You want camping? The park, dawn, a thermos, a bench by the lake, and a heron who's been there longer than the city. That's camping. That's the whole trip.
Rode out to the beach to sleep in the dunes once. Fog came in, the bike rusted, I got a cold, the sunrise was unbelievable. Would recommend. Would not repeat.
offair: Spent the morning at the jeweller's bench. Silver, a little brass, an ear cuff shaped like a fern. It's for Tomas. He doesn't know yet. Don't tell him.
I make harnesses, vests, tool belts, utility belts, anything with straps and pockets. People ask what for. For carrying things, sweetheart. What's your bag for.
The heron at Stow Lake was there again. Same bank, same bench, same me. I've got nine hundred photos of that bird. Nine hundred and one now. He blinked.
I ride a BMX everywhere. People say get a real bike. This is a real bike. It fits in the elevator. It fits in the club. It goes down stairs. Yours doesn't.
Skated the plaza till the sun came up with the crew, then rode to the botanical garden and looked at a tree fern for twenty minutes. Balance. That's balance.
Somebody said something about my friend Marco in the club. I won't say what I said. I'll say he's not coming back and the bouncer was very polite about it.
Twenty-nine, single, booked solid, and the happiest I've been. The friends are the point. The belts are how I say it.
There's a magnolia in the park that flowers for about nine days in February. I take the morning off for it every year. It's not optional. It's my church.
callers: This one's for Tomas, who's closing the shop with the door open and the radio on. Lock it this time, baby. Please. Love you.
Somebody called to ask about the heron. The heron's fine. The heron is thriving. Thank you for asking about the heron. Nobody asks about me.
Caller says: Dez, you sound like you've had too much coffee. Sweetheart, I've had the right amount of coffee. This is the right amount. Here's a tune.
Shout-out to the kid who fixed my chain at the skate spot and didn't say a word about my bike. That's grace. That's the whole thing. This one's yours.
For Marco, for Priya, for Tomas, for the whole crew in the second room right now: I can hear you from here. Turn it up. I'm coming after the show.
ads: The Loft is brought to you by The Loft, the sewing room. Harnesses, vests, belts, anything with straps, cut to you. Come up. Elevator's broken. Worth it.
Rosa's Fabric, in the district, closing at six. Canvas, webbing, buckles, the good thread. She will not sell you the wrong thing. She will tell you.
Tomas's Repair, at the skate spot. Bikes, boards, trucks, bearings. Open late. Honest. Cute. I'm allowed to say cute. He's my friend.
Silver from the bench. Ear cuffs, rings, the fern, the heron. One of a kind, because I can't make the same thing twice. That's a feature.
banter: Marisol on eighty-eight one is playing something slow for the harbour. Marisol. Sweetheart. The harbour can wait. The city cannot.
Kit's up on the ridge in a van going a hundred and seventy a minute. Kit, baby, we're going one twenty-eight down here and we have an elevator. It's broken. Come anyway.
Tess at The Roadhouse says she doesn't dance. Tess. I have seen you dance. In the redwoods. At four. You were efficient. I respect it.
The harbour, the hill, the farm, the bar and the loft. Five stations. The others go to bed. We're on till two. Then I ride home.
night: The city at two in the morning is the most honest thing I know. All the lights are for nobody. Drive like they're for you.
After the show I ride down the boulevard with the lights timed. Twelve greens in a row if you hit it right. I'm not racing. I'm dancing, slowly, on a bicycle.
There's an hour when the clubs let out and the whole street is people holding each other up. That's my favourite hour. That's why the show ends at two.
Nobody needs a reason to be out this late. You need a working front light and a friend who'll text back. I've got both. Here's a tune.
Whatever somebody said tonight about you, about your car, about your friends: they're not here. You are. I am. Go home loud.
It's three in the morning and this is a recording. I'm home, the bike's by the door, the needle's threaded for tomorrow. Night, city. Mind the tram tracks.
